title: Magnetic Poles
keyIdea: Every magnet has two poles, a north pole (N) and a south pole (S), where its pull is strongest. A freely hanging magnet turns until its north pole points north. When two magnets meet, like poles repel (N and N, or S and S, push apart) and unlike poles attract (N and S pull together).
familyTip: With two fridge magnets or bar magnets, let your child guess first: will these two ends push or pull? Then flip one magnet and try again. Ask them to explain the result using the words like and unlike poles.

visual.caption: Two magnets come close. Will these poles pull together or push apart? Drag each pair, or tap it then a box.

items: A south end meets a north end

lab.caption: Flagship lab: swing a magnet to north, push and pull poles, fill a results table, test clips, name a mystery magnet's poles.

kid: A magnet has two ends called poles. One is the north pole, N. The other is the south pole, S.
Hang a magnet so it can turn. It stops with its N pole pointing north. That is how a compass works.
Put two magnets end to end. N and S pull together. We say unlike poles attract. N and N push apart. So do S and S. We say like poles repel. You can feel the push.
The pull is strongest at the poles. That is why paper clips cling to the ends, not the middle.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. England NC Year 3 forces and magnets: describe magnets as having two poles, and predict whether two magnets will attract or repel each other depending on which poles are facing. NGSS 3-PS2-3 covers the same magnetic interactions.

A freely suspended magnet lines up with Earth's magnetic field, so the end that points north is called the north-seeking pole, shortened to north pole. The field, and so the pull, is strongest at the poles.

Common mistakes: thinking like poles attract; thinking N and S are like plus and minus charges; expecting the strongest pull in the middle; thinking a broken magnet keeps one pole per piece, when each piece gets an N and an S; and treating attraction as proof of a magnet, when plain iron is attracted too. Only repulsion proves it.

In the lab your child swings a magnet to north, feels attraction and repulsion by dragging, fills a four-row results table, dips the ends and middle in clips, and uses repulsion to name the poles of an unlabelled magnet.

practice.prompt: An N pole faces an S pole. What happens?
practice.hint: N and S are different poles. Are they like or unlike?
practice.explain: N and S are unlike poles, and unlike poles attract. The magnets pull together.

practice.prompt: A box holds {a} bar magnets. How many poles are there in total?
practice.hint: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.
practice.explain: Each magnet has 2 poles, so {a} magnets have {=2*a} poles.

practice.prompt: You test a bar magnet with clips. The two ends hold {a} clips each and the middle holds {b}. How many clips in all?
practice.hint: Two ends with the same number each, then add the middle.
practice.explain: The ends hold {a} + {a} = {=2*a} and the middle adds {b}, so {=2*a+b} clips. Most cling at the poles.

practice.prompt: An S pole faces another S pole. What happens?
practice.hint: Both ends are S. Same poles behave the same way as N and N.
practice.explain: S and S are like poles, and like poles repel. They push apart just as N and N do.

practice.prompt: A bar magnet hangs from a thread and stops turning. Where does its N pole point?
practice.hint: The poles were named after the way they point.
practice.explain: A freely hanging magnet lines up so its north-seeking pole points north. That is why it is called the north pole.

pool.prompt: Where is the pull of a bar magnet strongest?
pool.hint: Think about where the paper clips stuck.
pool.explain: The pull is strongest at the poles, the two ends. Hardly any clips stick to the middle.

pool.prompt: You snap {a} bar magnets in half. How many poles do all the pieces have?
pool.hint: Each half becomes a whole magnet with its own N and S.
pool.explain: Each magnet makes 2 pieces with 2 poles each, so 4 poles per magnet: {a} × 4 = {=4*a} poles.

pool.prompt: {a} magnets in a row all point north when they hang free. How many N poles point north?
pool.hint: Each magnet has exactly one north pole.
pool.explain: Every free magnet turns one N pole to the north, so {a} N poles point north.

pool.prompt: Ben says, 'N and N will stick together because they match.' Is he right?
choices: Only if the magnets are big
pool.hint: Try it with the lab: what did N meeting N do?
pool.explain: Ben has it the wrong way round. Like poles, such as N and N, push apart. Unlike poles attract.

pool.prompt: A metal bar is pulled towards BOTH ends of your magnet. What is it?
pool.hint: Would a magnet be pulled by both of your poles?
pool.explain: A magnet would push away one of your poles. Plain iron is pulled by both, so a pull alone proves nothing.

pool.prompt: End A of a mystery magnet pushes away your N pole. What is end A?
pool.hint: Which poles push each other away?
pool.explain: Only like poles repel. End A pushed your N away, so end A is a north pole too.

pool.prompt: Which test proves an object is a magnet?
choices: It pushes away one pole of a magnet
pool.hint: Iron is pulled too. What can only a magnet do?
pool.explain: A magnet pulls iron as well as other magnets, so only a push, repulsion, proves the object is a magnet.

pool.prompt: You flip one magnet round. The ends were pulling. What happens now?
pool.hint: Flipping one magnet swaps which pole faces the other.
pool.explain: They were unlike poles. After the flip the facing poles are alike, so they repel.

pool.prompt: Put the steps in order to find the N pole of an unlabelled magnet.
items: Bring your magnet's N pole near one end
Watch for a push or a pull
If it pushes, that end is N
pool.explain: Bring your N pole close, watch what happens, and use the push: like poles repel, so a push means that end is N.
